clips.text: Look at these two branching shapes. On the left, each fork splits in two, then in two again. On the right, one fork spreads straight into six tips. Could a symmetry score mistake a tree made from these for a perfectly balanced tree?

These are rooted trees. The top point is the root. Each line leads to a child, and a point with no children is a leaf. The picture records branching relationships, not the physical lengths of the lines.
Here, fully symmetric has a precise meaning. At every fork, all the child trees must have the same shape. Both of these separate trees pass that test. But their shapes are different from each other.
Now give every point a weight. For our first example, use the number of children plus one. A leaf weighs one. A point with two children weighs three. A point with six children weighs seven.
Add the weights on the left. There are three branching points, each worth three, and four leaves, each worth one. Three plus six plus four makes thirteen. We will call this sum the weighted size.
On the right, the root weighs seven and the six leaves contribute six. That also makes thirteen. Different shapes have landed on exactly the same number. This is a collision between weighted sizes.

Build a new tree by putting these two trees under a new root. Its left child has weighted size thirteen. Its right child also has weighted size thirteen. So a comparison of the two sizes sees no imbalance.

Inside each child, every fork was already symmetric. Every local comparison therefore returns zero. Adding all those zeros still gives zero, even though the new root joins two different shapes. You can see the mistake directly.

A Colless-like index adds these local differences. It is called sound if zero happens exactly for fully symmetric trees. Our example breaks soundness for this weight rule. Soundness concerns the zero score, not the ranking of every other tree.

Perhaps we only chose bad weights. Could larger whole numbers avoid every collision? The theorem says no. Whatever nonnegative whole-number weights you choose, some pair of different symmetric trees will share a weighted size.

To see why, first describe a symmetric tree by its branching recipe. The list two, three means two children at the first level, then three children at the next. There are two times three, or six leaves.

Reverse that recipe to three, two. The shape changes: three branches come first, rather than two. But the leaf count is still six. Multiplication forgets the order of the recipe, while the tree remembers it.

For the counting proof, use the numbers two, three and four. With one of each, there are six different orders. Every order gives twenty-four leaves. These are six different symmetric trees with the same leaf count.

Next take two copies of each number. There are ninety different recipes. In general, take m copies of each. Their leaf count is twenty-four to the power m. We need to count how many distinct recipes share it.

If all three m positions were different, there would be three m factorial arrangements. Factorial means multiplying down to one. But the m copies of two are interchangeable, and so are the threes and fours. Divide by m factorial three times.

This exact count is not twenty-seven to the power m. That number counts every string of length three m using three symbols, including unbalanced mixtures. Our balanced mixture is the largest group when strings are sorted by their three symbol counts.

There are only a quadratic number of those groups. So our count is at least twenty-seven to the power m, divided by that quadratic factor. The factor slows growth, but it cannot permanently defeat the larger exponential base.

Now count the possible weighted sizes. First remove the leaves. Every tree in the family has exactly the same number, so their total leaf weight is identical. Subtracting that common contribution preserves every equality between sizes.
What remains is the internal sum. Each point there has two, three or four children. Let M be the largest of those three weights. The number of internal points is smaller than the number of leaves.

You can see this bound by looking upwards from the leaves. Each earlier level has at most half as many points as the next. Even adding every internal level gives fewer points than the leaf level alone.

The internal sum is therefore a whole number between zero and M times twenty-four to the power m. Think of those integers as numbered boxes. Each recipe must go into the box matching its internal sum.

When there are more recipes than boxes, two recipes must share a box. Here is that pigeonhole principle on a small illustration: four objects cannot occupy three boxes without a collision. The proof applies the same idea to enormous trees.

For a concrete comparison, set M equal to five. The graph shows the exact recipe count divided by the upper bound on boxes. Above one, a collision is forced. The count eventually crosses because twenty-seven grows faster than twenty-four.

That crossing does not rely on M being five. Any fixed choice of M is eventually beaten. Two different symmetric trees then have the same internal sum, the same leaf contribution, and therefore the same total weighted size.

Join the colliding trees under one root, just as before. Every local comparison gives zero, but the root has different child shapes. This completes a hand proof for all nonnegative integer weight functions, not just the examples a computer checked.

The precise theorem is stronger. The weights at two, three and four only need to be whole multiples of one positive unit. Divide by that unit and the boxes are integers again. Rational weights are included.

The leaf weight need not fit that unit. It cancels because the leaf counts agree. Other branching weights do not enter this counting family. These restrictions matter: the result does not say that every possible weight rule fails.

Mir, Rotger and Rossello proposed the whole-number conjecture in 2018. They already gave some collisions, including one for powers of two, and sound irrational weight rules. This result is the universal impossibility proof, not the first example of a collision.

What about weights built from two independent units, such as one and the square root of two? Then our boxes become a grid. This counting argument no longer forces a collision. Whether some such rule is sound remains unsettled here.

Remember the three steps. Different symmetric trees can share a size. Equal sizes hide an asymmetric join. And counting forces that collision for every allowed whole-number rule. Correctness confidence is high; originality confidence is moderate, because the literature search was bounded.

The paper and its example checker accompany this video. The general theorem is a written mathematical proof; the small checks are illustrations, not its replacement. Valyu Research, 2026. Narration uses a synthetic voice.
